description: Growable lists and key-value maps — Java's everyday data structures.

screens.body:
Arrays lock their size at creation. In real programs you rarely know how many items you'll have — user input, database rows, API results. Collections solve that: they resize themselves.

The two you'll use daily: ArrayList (an ordered, growable list) and HashMap (key-value pairs, like a dictionary).

Think of it this way: arrays are for when you know the size; collections are for everything else.

options: Grow and shrink as you add/remove

screens.heading: Arrays are fixed — collections grow

screens.body:
Create one with its item type in angle brackets: ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(). The <> on the right is the 'diamond' — Java copies the type from the left.

Add with add(), read with get(index), count with size(), remove with remove(index). Indexes start at 0, like arrays and JS.

The #1 beginner mistake: calling length() on an ArrayList. Arrays use .length; ArrayList uses .size(). They will not forgive the mix-up.

options: How many items are in the list
check.question: names.size() returns…

screens.heading: ArrayList: the growable list
screens.keyPoint: add, get, size, remove — and it's size(), not length.

screens.body:
ArrayList<String> means 'a list that ONLY holds Strings.' Try adding an int and the compiler stops you — the bug is caught before the program runs instead of exploding halfway through.

One catch: generics need object types, not primitives. You can't write ArrayList<int> — it won't compile. Use the wrapper class Integer instead (same for Double, Boolean, Character).

Java quietly converts between int and Integer when needed — called autoboxing — so code like scores.add(95) on an ArrayList<Integer> just works.

options: Generics need object types — use Integer
check.question: Why won't `ArrayList<int>` compile?

code.snippet:
ArrayList<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();
scores.add(95); // int auto-boxed into Integer

screens.heading: Generics: the <Type> in angle brackets
screens.keyPoint: Generics need object types: Integer, not int.

screens.body:
A HashMap stores pairs: a key and the value under it. HashMap<String, Integer> scores maps names to numbers — scores.put("ada", 95) files 95 under 'ada'.

Look values up with get(key): scores.get("ada") returns 95. Ask for a missing key and you get null — Java's 'nothing here.'

Keys must be unique: putting a second value under 'ada' overwrites the first. It's the same idea as a JavaScript object: { ada: 95 }.
screens.heading: HashMap: keys point to values

screens.body:
Java's enhanced for loop walks a whole collection without indexes: for (String n : names) reads as 'for each name n in names.' Clean, no off-by-one errors.

For a HashMap, loop over map.keySet() to visit every key, then get() each value. Or use map.values() if you only care about values.

You'll still see classic index loops for arrays — but for collections, the enhanced for is the default choice.
screens.heading: Looping the easy way

screens.body:
Gotcha one: comparing Strings with == checks whether they're the same OBJECT, not the same text. Two equal-looking Strings can fail ==. Always compare text with .equals(): name.equals("ada").

Gotcha two: get() on a missing HashMap key returns null. Calling a method on that null — scores.get("nobody").toString() — throws a NullPointerException.

Both are rites of passage. Now that you've read this, you get to skip the painful version of learning them.
screens.heading: Two classic gotchas

screens.body:
You already know these structures — Java just names them differently. An ArrayList<String> is a JS array with a type label: add() is push(), get(i) is [i], size() is .length.

A HashMap<String, Integer> is a JS object (or a JS Map): put(k, v) is obj[k] = v, get(k) is obj[k]. The mental model transfers completely.

So when Java code feels heavy, translate it in your head: 'oh, this is just an array of strings.' It usually is.
